warmup.q: settleAll() calls this.settle(id) for each batch, and settle is annotated @Transactional. The same class runs as a Spring Boot bean and as a Quarkus @ApplicationScoped bean. Does each settle call start a transaction?
options: Yes in both: the annotation is on the method
No in Spring, yes in Quarkus
Yes in Spring, no in Quarkus
No in both: self-calls never pass a proxy
warmup.why: Spring's proxy, JDK or CGLIB, forwards to a separate target object, so this.settle inside the target never passes the proxy. Quarkus ArC intercepts the bean through a generated subclass that is the bean itself, and its docs say self-interception works (as a non-standard extension of CDI). The answer depends on where the real object lives, not on the annotation.

sections.h: A subclass proxy wraps a class by overriding its methods
sections.html:
A JDK proxy needs an interface. Plenty of beans have none, so frameworks generate a subclass instead. Here is one written by hand, for the demo's SettlementService:

Java
class TimedSettlementService extends SettlementService {
    @Override
    public String settle(String batch) {
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return super.settle(batch);                   // the original body, on THIS object
        } finally {
            log("settle", System.nanoTime() - t0);
        }
    }
    // audit() the same way; region() is final, so there is nothing to override
}
Kotlin
class TimedSettlementService : KSettlementService() {   // needs `open class`
    override fun settle(batch: String): String {             // needs `open fun`
        val t0 = System.nanoTime()
        try {
            return super.settle(batch)                       // the original body, on THIS object
        } finally {
            log("settle", System.nanoTime() - t0)
        }
    }
    // audit() the same way; region() is final, so there is nothing to override
}

Every method the subclass overrides becomes a place to add behaviour, and super.settle(batch) runs the original body on the same object. Byte Buddy writes this class at run time, for any class and any set of methods:

Java
Class<? extends SettlementService> sub = new ByteBuddy()
        .subclass(SettlementService.class)
        .method(isDeclaredBy(SettlementService.class))            // which methods to override
        .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration()
                .filter(named("intercept"))
                .to(new InSubclass()))                            // who handles them
        .make()
        .load(SettlementService.class.getClassLoader())
        .getLoaded();
Kotlin
val sub: Class<out KSettlementService> = ByteBuddy()
    .subclass(KSettlementService::class.java)
    .method(isDeclaredBy(KSettlementService::class.java))         // which methods to override
    .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration()
        .filter { it.name == "intercept" }
        .to(KInSubclass()))                                       // who handles them
    .make()
    .load(KSettlementService::class.java.classLoader)
    .loaded

The demo prints the result: a public class named ...SettlementService$ByteBuddy$nsokwLlA (the suffix is random on every run) that declares settle, audit, and two accessors such as settle$accessor$cvePe5kh. The accessors are how the interceptor's @SuperCall Callable runs super.settle(...), the line you wrote by hand above. The interceptor receives @Origin Method for the method being called. Byte Buddy binds parameters by these annotations.

A subclass can only intercept what it can override, and that sets the rules every subclass proxy lives by. A final class can't be subclassed at all. A final or private method isn't overridden, so it runs as written and nothing intercepts it: in the demo, region() just works, uncounted. And the subclass's constructor calls the superclass constructor, unless the framework skips it.

Kotlin turns the first rule into a daily problem, because classes and members are final unless you write open. Byte Buddy refuses a plain Kotlin class with Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. The Kotlin all-open compiler plugin "makes classes and their members open at compile time without requiring the open keyword", for classes carrying annotations you choose.

Byte Buddy is the library most of the ecosystem uses for this; 1.18.17 is the current release. The older cglib's own README says it "is unmaintained and does not work well (or possibly at all?) in newer JDKs, particularly JDK17+" and points to Byte Buddy. Spring keeps working because it ships its own patched copy, repackaged as org.springframework.cglib, along with Objenesis.

code.title: TwoModelsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l05; import net.bytebuddy.ByteBuddy; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.MethodDelegation; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.AllArguments; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.Origin; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.RuntimeType; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.SuperCall; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.isDeclaredBy; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named; /** The same subclass proxy, two models: the proxy IS the object, or the proxy forwards to a target. */ public class TwoModelsDemo { static final List<String> LOG = new ArrayList<>(); public static class SettlementService { static int constructed; public SettlementService() { constructed++; } public String settle(String batch) { return "settled " + batch + " (" + this.audit(batch) + ")"; } // self-call public String audit(String batch) { return "audited " + batch; } public final String region() { return "eu-west"; } } /** ArC-style: the generated subclass instance is the bean; @SuperCall runs the original body on it. */ public static class InSubclass { @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @SuperCall Callable<?> original) throws Exception { LOG.add("intercepted " + m.getName()); return original.call(); } } /** Spring-style: the generated subclass forwards to a separate target object. */ public static class Forwarding { private final Object target; public Forwarding(Object target) { this.target = target; } @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @AllArguments Object[] args) throws Exception { LOG.add("forwarded " + m.getName()); return m.invoke(target, args); } } static <T> Class<? extends T> subclass(Class<T> type, Object interceptor) { return new ByteBuddy().subclass(type) .method(isDeclaredBy(type)) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")) // bind to intercept() only, not equals() etc. .to(interceptor)) .make().load(type.getClassLoader()).getLoaded(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Class<? extends SettlementService> sub = subclass(SettlementService.class, new InSubclass()); System.out.println("generated " + sub.getName()); System.out.println("declares " + Arrays.stream(sub.getDeclaredMethods()).map(Method::getName).sorted().toList()); SettlementService bean = sub.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); System.out.println(bean.settle("B-17") + ", region " + bean.region()); System.out.println("subclass model: " + LOG); LOG.clear(); SettlementService.constructed = 0; SettlementService target = new SettlementService(); SettlementService proxy = subclass(SettlementService.class, new Forwarding(target)) .getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); System.out.println(proxy.settle("B-18")); System.out.println("forwarding model: " + LOG + ", constructors run: " + SettlementService.constructed); try { new ByteBuddy().subclass(KotlinFinalService.class).make(); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("Kotlin class without open: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

The last line is Kotlin class without open: Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types: class ...KotlinFinalService; after adding open, that line disappears because make() succeeds. In javap, settle and audit are plain public, while region() is public final: kotlinc keeps a member final unless you mark it open, even inside an open class.

sections.h: Where the real object lives decides whether self-calls are intercepted
sections.html:
Decorator and Proxy blamed self-invocation on proxies in general. The demo shows it's more specific than that. The same Byte Buddy subclass, built two ways, gives opposite answers for settle("B-17"), whose body calls this.audit(batch).

In the first model, the generated subclass instance is the object. There's no separate target. The interceptor runs the original body through @SuperCall, on that same instance. When the body calls this.audit(...), this is the subclass, the call dispatches virtually to its override, and the interceptor runs again. The log reads [intercepted settle, intercepted audit].

In the second model, the subclass instance is only a front for a separate target object. By hand, it looks like this:

Java
class ForwardingSettlementService extends SettlementService {
    private final SettlementService target;
    ForwardingSettlementService(SettlementService target) { this.target = target; }

    @Override
    public String settle(String batch) {
        log("settle");
        return target.settle(batch);                     // the body runs on the target
    }
    // audit() the same way
}
Kotlin
class ForwardingSettlementService(private val target: KSettlementService) : KSettlementService() {
    override fun settle(batch: String): String {
        log("settle")
        return target.settle(batch)                      // the body runs on the target
    }
    // audit() the same way
}

The demo's Forwarding interceptor does the same with method.invoke(target, args). The body runs on the target, whose this is the target, so this.audit(...) is an ordinary call that the proxy never sees. The log reads [forwarded settle]. The demo also counts constructors: two, because the target was built once and the proxy subclass was built with newInstance, which runs the superclass constructor again. That's the "constructor called twice" that Spring's 3.2 documentation warned about.

So "it's a subclass" doesn't settle the question. Ask where the state and the body run. If the proxy is the object, self-calls are intercepted, final methods still run on the real state, and fields are real. If the proxy forwards, self-calls skip it, and anything the proxy can't override runs on the proxy object itself, with whatever fields that object has. The lab tests this last point: a forwarding proxy's final method reads the proxy's own desk field ("unset"), not the target's ("London").

The frameworks you use pick different models. Spring AOP always forwards, whether it built a JDK proxy or a CGLIB subclass. Quarkus ArC intercepts with a generated subclass, and its documentation says self-interception works. The next two sections take them one at a time, from their documentation. This track ran neither framework; the Byte Buddy demo stands in for both models.

With audit final, the subclass model logs only [intercepted settle]: Byte Buddy can't override audit, so the self-call runs the original directly. sections.h: Spring AOP puts a JDK proxy or a CGLIB subclass in front of a separate target
sections.html:
Spring's reference documentation says it in one rule: "If the target object to be proxied implements at least one interface, a JDK dynamic proxy is used, and all of the interfaces implemented by the target type are proxied. If the target object does not implement any interfaces, a CGLIB proxy is created which is a runtime-generated subclass of the target type." Spring Boot changes the default. Its AopAutoConfiguration enables class-based proxies unless you set spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false (true in Boot 3.5.x and on main). So in a Boot application, expect CGLIB subclasses even for beans with interfaces. Spring Framework 7.0 adds @Proxyable(INTERFACES) and @Proxyable(TARGET_CLASS) to choose per bean.

Either way, the proxy forwards to a separate target bean. Spring calls the code a proxy runs around a method advice, and a method that gets it is "advised". The rules follow from the previous section, and the docs list them for CGLIB proxies: "final classes cannot be proxied", "final methods cannot be advised", "private methods cannot be advised", and package-private methods in a parent class from another package can't be advised either. The constructor is no longer called twice, because Spring creates the CGLIB instance through Objenesis, which skips constructors. That also means a final method, which runs on the proxy object itself, sees a proxy whose fields were never initialized.

For @Transactional the documentation spells out the consequences of proxy mode (the default): "only external method calls coming in through the proxy are intercepted", so self-invocation "does not lead to an actual transaction at runtime". The proxy must also be fully initialized, so don't rely on it in @PostConstruct. For class-based proxies, since Spring 6.0 protected and package-visible methods can be transactional too. Interface-based proxies need public methods declared in the interface. The documented ways out of self-invocation, best first: restructure so the call crosses a bean boundary, inject the bean into itself, or ("highly discouraged") AopContext.currentProxy(). AspectJ mode weaves the advice into your class instead, so there is no proxy at all.

Kotlin adds one more requirement. The kotlin-spring compiler plugin is "a preconfigured wrapper around the all-open plugin". It opens classes annotated with @Component, @Async, @Transactional, @Cacheable and @SpringBootTest, and, through the @Component meta-annotation, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController and @Configuration. Projects from start.spring.io enable it by default. Without it, a Kotlin bean is a final class that CGLIB can't subclass. If you write open class by hand and forget open fun, you get the quieter failure: methods that are never advised.

sections.h: Quarkus ArC generates its subclasses at build time, and Hibernate makes lazy ones
sections.html:
Quarkus's CDI container, ArC, generates its proxy classes while the application builds, not at startup. Its processor names them in comments in its own source: "Foo_Subclass extends Foo implements Subclass" for an intercepted bean, and "Foo_ClientProxy extends Foo implements ClientProxy" for a client proxy. Both are subclasses of your bean class, playing two roles.

A client proxy stands in for a normal-scoped bean, one whose instance belongs to a scope such as @ApplicationScoped or @RequestScoped. The docs call it "an object that delegates all method invocations to a target bean instance". It's the forwarding model, used for laziness and scoping: the real instance is created on the first method call, which is also why the docs say to "never read or write a field of a normal scoped bean" from outside. A @Singleton bean has no client proxy.

The intercepted subclass is the other model. The Quarkus CDI reference says: "Quarkus supports what is known as intercepted self-invocation or just self-interception - a scenario where CDI bean invokes its own intercepted method from within another method while triggering any associated interceptors." It calls this a non-standard feature, because the CDI specification doesn't define it. Given the generated Foo_Subclass extends Foo, the natural reading is that the subclass instance is the contextual instance (the bean object ArC created for that scope), so this.doSomething() dispatches to the intercepting override. That mechanism is an inference from the docs and the class names; this track didn't trace it in ArC's source. The behaviour is documented. A client proxy in front of an intercepted bean forwards to that subclass instance, so both apply at once.

ArC also works around Kotlin's finality. quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes is true by default, and lets Quarkus proxy final classes and classes with final methods. The Quarkus Kotlin guide still configures all-open for @Path, @ApplicationScoped and JPA entities. Follow the guide, and check with javap and a test before assuming either is unnecessary. Private members are reached by reflection, so the docs recommend package-private instead.

Hibernate's lazy proxies are generated at run time with Byte Buddy (ByteBuddyProxyFactory). A proxy "masquerades as a real entity", but holds no state until you call a method, and after the session ends that call throws LazyInitializationException. Its rules are the subclass rules: an entity "must be a non-final class, with a non-private constructor with no parameters", collection fields must use interface types, and "instanceof and typecasts do not work correctly" on a proxy for a polymorphic association, unless you pay for @ConcreteProxy. Your equals() "must be written to accommodate the possibility that the object passed to the equals() might be a proxy". For Kotlin entities, the kotlin-jpa plugin opens them and adds the no-argument constructor.

Check yourself before the lab: a Payment loaded lazily through an association is a Hibernate proxy. What does payment.getClass() == Payment.class return, and what happens to an equals that starts with if (getClass() != o.getClass()) return false? (The first is false, because the object is an instance of the generated subclass, so that equals says a proxy and the real row differ.)

analogy: Think of two ways to give a clerk a supervisor. In the first, the supervisor sits inside the clerk's own desk: every request, including the ones the clerk makes to themselves ("let me audit this first"), passes the supervisor. That's Quarkus ArC's intercepted subclass, and Byte Buddy's @SuperCall. In the second, the supervisor sits at a front counter and passes requests back to the clerk, who then talks to themselves in private. That's Spring's proxy. The analogy breaks on the front counter's own desk: a forwarding proxy is also a full copy of the clerk's class, with its own empty drawers. Anything it can't pass back, a final method, quietly runs at the counter, using those empty drawers.
world: Moving a payments service from Spring Boot to Quarkus can change behaviour without one edited line. A @Transactional ledger method called from the same bean was silently non-transactional under Spring and becomes transactional under ArC, so a batch that used to commit row by row now commits per call, and lock times change. The reverse migration loses transactions instead. In Kotlin, the plugin setup decides whether a bean can be proxied at all: kotlin-spring (or a Spring Initializr project) for Spring, and all-open as the Quarkus Kotlin guide recommends, plus kotlin-jpa for Hibernate entities. Check the generated class with javap rather than trusting the annotation you can see.
mistake: The most common mistake is believing an interceptor annotation is part of the method, so it must apply on every call. It applies only when the call passes through generated code that can override the method. In a Spring bean that rules out self-calls, private methods, and in Kotlin every method you didn't mark open and the kotlin-spring plugin didn't open. People make it because the annotation sits right on the method, the code compiles, and unit tests that call the class directly can't tell the difference. The fix is to know which model your container uses, keep advised methods open and called from outside the bean (or rely on ArC's documented self-interception in Quarkus), and test through the container with an assertion on the effect, such as a rolled-back row.

compare.title: A timing subclass proxy in Java and Kotlin

java.title: TimedSubclass.java
java.html: public class SuperCallTimer { @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @SuperCall Callable<?> original) throws Exception { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { return original.call(); // the original body, on this same object } finally { System.out.println(m.getName() + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) + " ns"); } } } // the service class is open by default in Java; final methods would be skipped FxQuoteService timed = new ByteBuddy() .subclass(FxQuoteService.class) .method(isPublic().and(isDeclaredBy(FxQuoteService.class))) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")).to(new SuperCallTimer())) .make().load(FxQuoteService.class.getClassLoader()).getLoaded() .getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();

kotlin.title: TimedSubclass.kt
kotlin.html: class SuperCallTimer { @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin m: Method, @SuperCall original: Callable<*>): Any? { val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { return original.call() // the original body, on this same object } finally { println("${m.name} took ${System.nanoTime() - t0} ns") } } } // FxQuoteService and each method must be `open` (or opened by all-open) val timed: FxQuoteService = ByteBuddy() .subclass(FxQuoteService::class.java) .method(isPublic<MethodDescription>().and(isDeclaredBy(FxQuoteService::class.java))) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")).to(SuperCallTimer())) .make().load(FxQuoteService::class.java.classLoader).loaded .getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()

compare.note: The Byte Buddy calls are identical. The language changes what there is to intercept. A Java class and its methods are open unless marked final. A Kotlin class and its members are final unless marked open, so the same builder silently skips every Kotlin method you didn't open, and refuses the class outright if the class itself is final. Kotlin also needs an explicit type argument for isPublic<MethodDescription>(), because the matcher is generic. In both, filter(named("intercept")) stops Byte Buddy from considering the interceptor's other methods (equals, toString) as delegation targets, which otherwise fails with "Cannot resolve ambiguous delegation".

worked.title: A @Transactional Kotlin method that never starts a transaction

steps.say: A Spring Boot service in Kotlin. Someone added open to the class so the proxy could be created, and the app starts fine. Before reading on: does settle run in a transaction when a controller calls it?
steps.code: @Service open class SettlementService(private val ledger: LedgerRepository) { @Transactional fun settle(batchId: String) { // no `open` ledger.post(batchId) } }

alt.html: // the Java equivalent of what kotlinc generated @Service public class SettlementService { private final LedgerRepository ledger; public SettlementService(LedgerRepository ledger) { this.ledger = ledger; } @Transactional public final void settle(String batchId) { // final: CGLIB can't override it ledger.post(batchId); } }

steps.say: Check the JVM shape. javap -p shows the class without final, which is why Spring could build its CGLIB subclass. settle is still public final void settle(java.lang.String). The Spring docs: "final methods cannot be advised". So the controller calls the proxy, the proxy can't override settle, and the inherited body runs on the proxy object, with no transaction.

It's worse than a missing transaction. The body runs on the proxy instance, not the target, and Spring creates CGLIB proxies through Objenesis, which skips constructors. On the proxy, ledger was never assigned. The forwarding test in this lesson's lab shows the same effect with Byte Buddy: a final method reads the proxy's own field, not the target's. Expect a NullPointerException on ledger, or silently wrong state.

Fix it at the build, not one method at a time. The kotlin-spring plugin opens @Service and @Transactional classes and their members, so settle compiles without final. Then keep calls to settle coming from outside the bean, because the proxy still forwards and a self-call would still skip it.
steps.code: // build.gradle.kts plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21" kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.4.21" // all-open preset for Spring annotations }

lab.title: Time a Kotlin class with Byte Buddy, two ways
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail with NotImplementedError.

In TimingProxies, write a private build(type, interceptor) that does ByteBuddy().subclass(type).method(isPublic<MethodDescription>().and(isDeclaredBy(type))).intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration().filter(named("intercept")).to(interceptor)).make().load(type.classLoader).loaded.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance().

Write a SuperCallInterceptor(clock, sink) class with @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin method: Method, @SuperCall zuper: Callable<*>): Any?. Read the clock, call zuper.call(), read the clock, record, and on an exception record failed = true and rethrow it. Use it in subclassTimed.

Run the tests. You should now get Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. Open FxQuoteService and its three quote methods, but leave deskName final. Run again and watch the self-call test pass.

Write a ForwardingInterceptor(target, clock, sink) whose intercept(@Origin method: Method, @AllArguments args: Array<Any?>) times method.invoke(target, *args) and unwraps InvocationTargetException. Use it in forwardingTimed. Run until all six pass.
hints: Cannot resolve ambiguous delegation ... to ... toString() or ... means Byte Buddy considered other methods of your interceptor. Keep the filter(named("intercept")).
The fake clock moves 1 ms per read. quote should record 5ms in the subclass model (its own two reads, plus two for each inner call) and 1ms in the forwarding model.
Interceptor classes must be public (Kotlin's default), because the generated class lives in a child loader and calls them from outside your package's code.
lab.done: All six tests in TimingProxiesTest pass, and deskName is still final.

drill.title: Which model, which result?
drill.prompt: Without looking: write the two Byte Buddy interceptors from memory, one that runs the original body on the same object and one that forwards to a target. Then answer: in each model, is this.audit() inside settle() intercepted, and what does a final method see?

answer.html: // 1. the proxy IS the object: self-calls intercepted, final methods run on real state public class InSubclass { @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @SuperCall Callable<?> original) throws Exception { return original.call(); } } // 2. the proxy forwards: self-calls skip it, final methods run on the proxy's own fields public class Forwarding { private final Object target; public Forwarding(Object target) { this.target = target; } @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @AllArguments Object[] args) throws Throwable { try { return m.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } } }

alt.html: // 1. the proxy IS the object: self-calls intercepted, final methods run on real state class InSubclass { @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin m: Method, @SuperCall original: Callable<*>): Any? = original.call() } // 2. the proxy forwards: self-calls skip it, final methods run on the proxy's own fields class Forwarding(private val target: Any) { @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin m: Method, @AllArguments args: Array<Any?>): Any? = try { m.invoke(target, *args) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } }

recap: Subclass proxies (Byte Buddy, Spring's CGLIB, ArC, Hibernate) wrap classes, but only what they can override: no final classes, no final or private methods.
Kotlin classes and members are final by default. Use open, all-open, kotlin-spring or kotlin-jpa, and check with javap -p.
Two models: the proxy is the object (ArC's _Subclass, @SuperCall), so self-calls are intercepted; or the proxy forwards to a target (Spring AOP), so self-calls skip it.
On a forwarding proxy, a method it can't override runs on the proxy object itself, with the proxy's own (often uninitialized) fields.
Spring uses a JDK proxy if the bean has interfaces and CGLIB otherwise, but Spring Boot defaults to class-based proxies. @Transactional in proxy mode ignores self-invocation.
Quarkus ArC builds proxies at build time and documents self-interception. Hibernate's lazy proxies need non-final entities with a no-arg constructor and proxy-aware equals.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Spring uses a CGLIB subclass, and a subclass overrides methods, so self-calls must be intercepted." Explain why that's wrong, why Quarkus behaves differently, and what Kotlin adds to the picture.
explain.answer: Being a subclass only tells you which methods can be intercepted. The question is which object runs the body. Spring's CGLIB proxy is a separate object that forwards each call to the target bean. The body runs on the target, where this is the target, so a call to this.settle() never reaches the proxy. Methods the proxy can't override, final or private ones, run on the proxy object itself, whose fields Objenesis never initialized. Quarkus ArC generates an intercepted subclass that is the bean instance, so this.settle() dispatches to the overriding method and the interceptors run; its docs call this self-interception. Kotlin makes classes and members final by default, so without open or the kotlin-spring or all-open plugin there's nothing to override. Then Spring can't proxy the class, or silently can't advise the method.

deeper.html:
Byte Buddy can also change a class instead of subclassing it. rebase(Clock.class) keeps the original method body under a new private name, now$original$..., and generates a new now that can call it. The Javadoc likens it to "creating a subclass where the subclass is later merged with the original class file". redefine(Clock.class) replaces now and discards the original body. Both produce a class with the original name, so you can only load them where the original isn't loaded yet, or rename them, or, in a running JVM, use an agent. That's lesson 7, where Byte Buddy's Advice comes in. Advice inlines your code into the existing method body instead of adding accessor methods and helper classes, which is what retransforming a loaded class requires.

The subclass's helper methods have a cost you can see. Each intercepted method gets an $accessor$ twin so the interceptor can call the original, and @SuperCall creates a small Callable per call. In this track's single JMH run, a Byte Buddy subclass with @SuperCall measured about 0.9 ns per call against 0.8 ns direct, and the JDK proxy about 4.3 ns. The numbers are noisy and indicative only, but the order is clear.

Quarkus can intercept some static methods too. The CDI reference allows an interceptor binding on a non-private static method, with three limits: only method-level bindings count, private static methods are never intercepted, and InvocationContext#getTarget() returns null. For producer methods whose result needs interceptors, InterceptionProxy generates, at build time, a subclass that intercepts and forwards. The class must not be final, must not have non-private final methods, and needs a non-private no-argument constructor. These are the subclass rules once again.
